Osier Willow.narrative: I was born in the hollow and learned the streams before I learned my letters, such as they are. My weirs have fed this house for thirty years, and I know every pool from the upper falls to the alder bend — which is why it galls me when Sorrel Fenwick's nets reach where my father's never did. The works in Kettlebridge send their smoke east over the forest, and some mornings the water tastes of it, and I say so to anyone who will hear. What the Old Green allows, the Eldest decides; but the streams are mine to speak for.

relations.name: Rush Willow
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the berries and the garden; I keep the water. Between us the house eats.

relations.name: Reed Willow
relations.label: son
relations.note: Quick with a trap already. He'll have the streams when I'm done with them.

relations.name: Sorrel Fenwick
relations.label: rival
relations.note: Her weirs block the run at the alder bend and she knows it.

relations.name: Reed Fenwick
relations.label: rival's son
relations.note: A decent lad, but he fishes his mother's side of the water and I've told him so.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Takes my smoked fish and pays fair; a man can do business with him.

relations.name: Vetch Quill
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Rush's friend; keeps her bees and her counsel, and doesn't meddle in the water quarrel.

relations.name: Yarrow Underbank
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Works fallen wood only, like the Old Green says. I'd trust him with a weir gate.

relations.name: Pipwort Bramblecap
relations.label: the Eldest
relations.note: She keeps the hollow's memory. When she rules on the timber, I'll hear her out.

memories.gist: My father walked me the whole stream from the upper falls to the alder bend, naming every pool and where the fish lie in each season.
The morning the Kettlebridge smoke first lay thick on the water and the fish tasted of it; I poured the catch back and went hungry rather than sell it.
Rush and I built the garden by the stream the first spring we were wed, and she planted the first berry canes while I set the first weir stakes.
Sorrel Fenwick set her weir below the alder bend without a word to anyone, and I found the run blocked and my traps empty for a week.
Reed brought home his first full creel at eight years old, grinning, and I pretended not to be proud and failed.

stances.why: My family has fished the upper pools for generations; the Fenwicks have no claim above the alder bend.
Hauling the old forest's fallen wood up the giants' track will foul the streams and the weirs, and the hollow needs its water more than the shelf needs roofs.
The Kettlebridge works foul the streams east of the forest, and I will say so to anyone who will hear.
The Old Green holds, and Pipwort keeps its memory; I'll argue my side but abide her ruling.
Alder Rush takes my smoked fish at a fair price, and a man who trades fair is worth keeping.

pastimes: mending and re-weaving the willow traps by the fire of an evening
walking the upper pools at first light to read the water
smoking fish over alder chips and trading the best of it at the hollow's stalls
Osier Willow.calling: I keep the weirs and read the streams; the water tells me what it needs, and I speak for it.

Rush Willow.narrative: I came to this house as a bride and planted the berry rows myself, and I have watched the old forest shrink a little each year since. Osier frets about his pools and Sorrel Fenwick's weirs, and I let him fret; my worry is the axe and the smoke and the wolves coming closer to the clearing. Vetch Quill and I talk of it over the hives. The hollow must eat, but the forest is what feeds it, and I will not see it cut to the stumps.

good relations with neighbours and the Eldest

relations.name: Osier Willow
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He frets at the water and I fret at the wood, and somehow the house holds.

relations.name: Reed Willow
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy. He wants the sea, and I want him to want the hollow, but I'll not hold him back.

relations.name: Vetch Quill
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We talk of the forest over her hives, and she sees it the same as I do.

relations.name: Sorrel Fenwick
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Osier's quarrel with her is not mine; she lost a husband and fishes to eat.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Takes our fish and our berries; a fair man with the hollow's store.

relations.name: Pipwort Bramblecap
relations.label: the Eldest
relations.note: She remembers when the forest was whole. I trust her to weigh the timber rightly.

relations.name: Yarrow Underbank
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He will not fell a living tree, and that is the right of it.

relations.name: Clover Mossfoot
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We argue about the seed rows, but she works hard and her flax is good.

memories.gist: The first spring in this house, planting the berry canes by the stream while Osier set weir stakes, and thinking the hollow was the whole world and enough.
Walking the forest edge with Vetch and finding the stumps where the Ferncross men had been, and the two of us resolving to speak at the common table.
Reed at eight, coming home with his first creel and a cut on his hand he was too proud to mention.
The winter the wolves came down to the berry rows and we kept the fire high all night and heard them in the dark beyond the garden.
The morning the smoke from Kettlebridge lay over the garden and the bees would not leave the hives, and I knew the forest was not as far from the works as we liked to think.

stances.why: The old forest feeds the hollow; if it is cut close there is no garden, no berries, no hollow.
The fallen wood is the hollow's own; the giants can wait until our own frames and gates are mended.
Neighbours you quarrel with are neighbours you cannot borrow from in a hard winter.
I have seen a thin winter and I will not see another if I can help it.
He is his father's son in the water and mine in the garden; whatever he chooses, he should choose it himself.

pastimes: tending the berry rows and the garden at dawn
sitting with Vetch Quill over the hives, talking of the forest
drying and storing berries and fibre for winter
Rush Willow.calling: I grow what feeds this house, and I mean the forest to still be standing when Reed's children eat from it.

Reed Willow.narrative: I help my father with the weirs and I know the streams nearly as well as he does, though he would say not yet. Reed Fenwick and I fish together sometimes, and it is awkward, because our mothers and fathers do not agree about the water. I want to see the sea at Lanternquay one day — the real sea, not the streams — and I think about it more than I should when there are traps to set.

relations.name: Osier Willow
relations.label: father
relations.note: He knows the streams better than anyone, and I want to know them like he does.

relations.name: Rush Willow
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She worries about the wolves and the wood, but she lets me go to the water.

relations.name: Reed Fenwick
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We fish together and I've told him his mother's weirs spread too far, and he took it better than his mother would.

relations.name: Sorrel Fenwick
relations.label: friend's mother
relations.note: She is sharp with my father, but she has been kind enough to me.

memories.gist: My father walking me the stream and showing me where the fish lie, and letting me set a trap myself for the first time.
Fishing the alder bend with Reed Fenwick and catching nothing, and laughing about it until our fathers called us home.
The night the wolves came down and my mother kept the fire high; I lay awake listening and was more excited than afraid.
A pedlar telling us of Lanternquay and the tide lanterns and the boats, and me thinking about it for days after.

stances.why: My father says so, and I have seen how the Fenwick weirs block the run.
The quarrel is between our parents, not between us, and I will not lose a friend to it.
There is a whole sea beyond the streams, and I mean to see it before I am old.

pastimes: fishing the alder bend with Reed Fenwick
setting and checking traps along the streams
listening to travellers' tales of the sea and the harbour at the hollow's edge
Reed Willow.calling: I want to learn the water the way my father knows it — and then see where it runs to.
